The invention relates to an application assembly for applying a coating material onto confectionery products, such as candies, chocolates, biscuits, wafers, or similar edible articles. The assembly is configured to receive a confectionery product and to apply a desired amount of coating material to one or more surfaces of the product in a controlled and efficient manner.

The application assembly includes a housing defining a product coating void. The product coating void is shaped and dimensioned to receive at least a portion of the confectionery product during a coating operation. In use, the confectionery product is positioned within the product coating void so that coating material can be directed toward and applied onto the product.

The assembly further includes at least one receptacle for receiving and holding coating material. The coating material may be any suitable edible coating, including chocolate, compound coating, glaze, sugar-based coating, flavored coating, or another flowable confectionery material. Each receptacle is arranged in fluid communication with the product coating void and includes a plurality of supply holes. The supply holes allow the coating material to flow from the receptacle into the product coating void, thereby delivering the coating material to the region in which the confectionery product is positioned.

Each receptacle also includes one or more applicator members. The applicator members are configured to contact, guide, spread, or otherwise transfer coating material onto the confectionery product. During operation, coating material supplied through the supply holes is received by or distributed along the applicator members, which then apply the coating material to the surface of the confectionery product. The applicator members may assist in achieving a uniform coating thickness, improving coverage, and reducing excess or uneven accumulation of coating material.

In addition, each applicator member includes a cavity configured to collect and store accumulated coating material. This cavity is particularly useful when a confectionery product remains static within the product coating void, for example during a pause in movement or processing. In such circumstances, excess coating material may accumulate near the applicator member. Rather than allowing the material to overflow, drip uncontrollably, or create an uneven deposit on the confectionery product, the cavity temporarily receives and stores the accumulated coating material. This helps maintain a cleaner coating process and contributes to more consistent coating quality.

Accordingly, the application assembly provides a controlled arrangement for delivering and applying coating material to confectionery products. By combining a housing with a product coating void, coating receptacles with supply holes, and applicator members having accumulation cavities, the assembly can improve coating distribution, manage excess material, and enhance the reliability and quality of confectionery coating operations.
outputs.L4:
The invention relates to an apparatus and method for applying partial coatings to confectionery products, such as chocolate articles, candy pieces, biscuits, wafers, bars, pralines, or similar edible products. More particularly, the invention concerns an application assembly configured to deliver coating material only to selected regions of a product, rather than covering the entire product surface. The coating material may be chocolate, compound coating, icing, glaze, caramel, fat-based coating, sugar-based coating, or any other flowable confectionery material suitable for transfer onto a product surface.

The application assembly includes a housing that supports and defines the operating components of the coating system. Within or adjacent to the housing, one or more coating receptacles are provided for receiving and holding a supply of coating material. The coating material is delivered from the receptacles through one or more supply holes formed in the housing. These supply holes communicate with corresponding applicator members, which are arranged to contact, approach, or otherwise cooperate with the confectionery product during a coating operation.

In use, a confectionery product is positioned so that a product coating void, recess, cavity, channel, or other defined coating region is aligned with the applicator members. The applicator members transfer coating material from the supply holes into the product coating void. In this way, the coating material is applied precisely to a desired portion of the product, while surrounding areas of the product remain substantially uncoated. The system is therefore especially suitable for products requiring decorative filling, striped or patterned coating, localized flavor zones, filled recesses, or controlled surface features.

A key feature of the invention is the provision of an applicator cavity associated with the applicator members. The applicator cavity is configured to collect, receive, and temporarily store excess coating material during operation. This is particularly advantageous when a confectionery product remains static relative to the application assembly, for example during indexing, pausing, alignment, or dwell time in a production process. Without such a cavity, coating material may continue to accumulate at the application point, leading to overfilling, smearing, dripping, stringing, or undesirable coating buildup on the product or on the apparatus.

The applicator cavity acts as a controlled reservoir for excess coating material. When coating material is supplied but is not immediately transferred to the product, the excess material is received in the cavity rather than being forced onto the product surface. When relative movement between the product and the applicator assembly resumes, or when the coating void is again positioned to accept coating material, the stored coating material may be transferred in a controlled manner from the applicator cavity to the product. This allows the apparatus to maintain a consistent coating volume and improves the accuracy and repeatability of partial coating application.

By collecting and storing excess coating material, the invention reduces unwanted accumulation of coating at the interface between the applicator members and the confectionery product. It also helps prevent contamination of non-coated product regions and minimizes waste of coating material. The arrangement can improve product appearance, reduce the need for cleaning, and increase reliability in high-speed confectionery manufacturing lines.

The housing, coating receptacles, supply holes, applicator members, and applicator cavity may be configured in various shapes and sizes depending on the type of confectionery product and the desired coating pattern. Multiple applicator members may be arranged in parallel or in a patterned configuration to apply coating to multiple voids or regions simultaneously. The supply holes may be dimensioned to regulate the flow rate of coating material, and the applicator cavity may be sized to accommodate expected excess coating volumes during pauses or static product conditions.

Overall, the invention provides a precise and controlled system for applying partial coatings to confectionery products. By incorporating an applicator cavity that manages excess coating material, the application assembly enables clean, repeatable coating transfer into defined product coating voids while reducing over-application, mess, and material waste.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called the definite article because it points to something specific. When we say “a book,” we may mean any book, but when we say “the book,” we mean a particular one that the speaker and listener both understand.

Although “the” may seem simple, it helps give sentences clarity and direction. It can refer to something already mentioned, something unique, or something known in context. For example, “the sun” refers to the specific star at the center of our solar system, while “the door” may refer to a door nearby or previously discussed.

The word “the” shows how even the smallest words can carry meaning. Without it, English would feel less precise and less natural. It reminds us that language is built not only from big, expressive words, but also from quiet, essential ones that hold sentences together.

## Invention Disclosure: Device and Method for Applying Partial Coatings to Confectionery Products

### Title  
**Device and Method for Partially Coating Confectionery Products Using a Coating Void Supplied by Coating Material from One or More Receptacles**

### Field of the Invention  
The present invention relates generally to confectionery processing equipment and methods. More particularly, the invention relates to a device and method for applying a partial coating to a confectionery product by introducing a flowable coating material from one or more receptacles into a coating void in which only a selected portion of the confectionery product is exposed to the coating material.

### Background  
Confectionery products, such as bars, pralines, biscuits, wafers, candies, frozen confections, and molded sweets, are often coated with chocolate, compound coatings, glazes, icings, caramel, yogurt coatings, fat-based coatings, sugar-based coatings, or other edible coating materials. Conventional coating techniques, including full enrobing, dipping, spraying, and drizzling, may cover an entire product surface or provide irregular decorative patterns.  

In many applications, however, it is desirable to apply a coating only to a defined region of a confectionery product, for example to a base portion, side portion, corner portion, band, stripe, edge, localized recess, or end portion. Existing methods for partial coating can involve mechanical dipping, masks, wiping elements, or complex handling systems, which may be difficult to clean, may lack precision, may cause product damage, or may be unsuitable for high-throughput production.

Accordingly, there is a need for a device and method capable of applying a controlled partial coating to confectionery products in a repeatable, hygienic, and efficient manner.

### Summary of the Invention  
In one aspect, the invention provides a coating device for applying a partial coating to a confectionery product. The device comprises a product support configured to support or convey a confectionery product, one or more receptacles configured to hold a flowable coating material, and a coating void positioned relative to the confectionery product such that only a predetermined portion of the confectionery product is exposed to coating material present in the coating void. The one or more receptacles are arranged to deliver coating material into the coating void, whereby the coating material contacts and coats only the exposed portion of the confectionery product.

In another aspect, the invention provides a method for partially coating a confectionery product. The method comprises positioning a confectionery product relative to a coating void, supplying a coating material from at least one receptacle into the coating void, allowing the coating material to contact a selected portion of the confectionery product, and removing or advancing the confectionery product such that the selected portion carries a partial coating.

In certain embodiments, the coating void is defined between a surface of the confectionery product and one or more boundary members of the device. In other embodiments, the coating void is defined by a cavity, channel, gap, recess, trough, chamber, or open volume into which the coating material flows. The dimensions of the coating void may be selected to determine the height, width, depth, thickness, or area of the partial coating.

The coating material may flow from the receptacle into the coating void by gravity, pressure, pumping, metering, vibration, capillary action, displacement, overflow, or a combination thereof. The coating material may be continuously or intermittently supplied. Excess coating material may be collected and recirculated.

### Detailed Description of Exemplary Embodiments  

#### General Construction  
A coating apparatus according to an embodiment of the invention comprises a frame supporting a product transport system and a coating station. The product transport system may include a conveyor belt, chain conveyor, pocket conveyor, rotating drum, indexed carrier, robotic gripper, tray, mold plate, or other support configured to present confectionery products to the coating station.

The coating station includes at least one receptacle for receiving and holding a flowable edible coating material. The receptacle may be a reservoir, hopper, cup, trough, manifold, dosing chamber, cartridge, pipe, tank, or other container suitable for food-grade coating material. The receptacle may include a heater, cooler, agitator, stirrer, level sensor, temperature sensor, viscosity control system, pump inlet, pump outlet, valve, or dosing element.

A coating void is located at or adjacent to the path of the confectionery products. The coating void is configured to receive coating material from the receptacle and to expose only a selected portion of the confectionery product to the coating material. The coating void may be open at one side to receive the product, or may be formed when the product is positioned adjacent to a forming surface. In use, the coating material occupies the coating void and contacts a portion of the confectionery product while other portions remain substantially uncoated.

#### Coating Void  
The coating void may be defined by one or more structural elements including walls, lips, rails, plates, guides, seals, spacers, dams, side members, or forming surfaces. In some embodiments, the coating void is a narrow gap between the confectionery product and a coating-forming member. In other embodiments, the coating void is a cavity into which a lower portion of the product is inserted. In further embodiments, the coating void is a side channel adjacent to the lateral edge of the product, enabling coating of one or more sides without coating the top surface.

The coating void may have a fixed geometry or an adjustable geometry. For example, at least one wall defining the coating void may be movable to adjust the coating height or coating thickness. Adjustable screws, cams, actuators, pneumatic cylinders, servo drives, or interchangeable inserts may be provided to adapt the coating void to different product dimensions.

The coating void may be shaped to apply a partial coating having a selected configuration, including but not limited to a stripe, band, base layer, side coating, end cap, corner coating, crescent, spot, frame, or decorative region. Multiple coating voids may be arranged in series or parallel to apply multiple coatings or differently colored coatings to different portions of a product.

#### Supply of Coating Material  
The receptacle is fluidly connected to the coating void. In one embodiment, the receptacle is positioned above the coating void such that coating material flows downwardly by gravity. In another embodiment, the receptacle is connected to the coating void via one or more conduits and a pump or metering device. The flow rate may be controlled by a valve, nozzle, slot, gate, pump speed, piston doser, auger, diaphragm pump, gear pump, peristaltic pump, or pressure regulator.

The coating material may be supplied to the coating void continuously to maintain a coating bath or meniscus at a defined level. Alternatively, the coating material may be supplied intermittently in synchronism with the arrival of individual confectionery products. The receptacle may include an overflow edge or weir to maintain a constant coating level in the coating void. Excess coating material may be discharged through an outlet, collected in a return receptacle, filtered, tempered, reheated, and recirculated.

In some embodiments, a plurality of receptacles supplies the same coating material to different regions of the coating void. In other embodiments, different receptacles supply different coating materials, for example dark chocolate, milk chocolate, white chocolate, colored compound coating, caramel, icing, or flavored coatings. Flow from different receptacles may be sequential, simultaneous, pulsed, or patterned.

#### Product Positioning  
The confectionery product may be positioned so that only a portion of the product intersects or bounds the coating void. For example, the product may be supported with a lower face partially immersed in coating material contained in the coating void. Alternatively, the product may pass adjacent to a coating channel so that one side wall is coated while the upper face remains exposed and uncoated.

The product support may include masking or shielding features that prevent coating material from contacting undesired surfaces. In certain embodiments, the support itself forms part of the coating void. For example, the product may be carried in a pocket having openings corresponding to regions to be coated. Coating material entering the coating void contacts the exposed product region through the opening while other regions remain shielded.

The apparatus may include registration elements for locating the confectionery product relative to the coating void. Such elements may include stops, guides, pockets, suction holders, side rails, clamps, magnetic holders, vacuum apertures, or optical positioning systems. Accurate positioning may ensure repeatable coating boundaries.

#### Removal and Finishing  
After contact with the coating material, the confectionery product is withdrawn, lifted, advanced, rotated, or otherwise separated from the coating void. The coated portion may carry a partial coating layer. The thickness of the coating may be influenced by residence time, coating viscosity, temperature, product speed, void dimensions, withdrawal angle, withdrawal speed, and optional air knives, scrapers, vibration devices, wipers, or drip-removal elements.

The apparatus may further include a cooling tunnel, setting station, crystallization zone, refrigeration station, or drying station downstream of the coating void to set or solidify the partial coating. The apparatus may also include inspection devices, weighing devices, cameras, or sensors for determining coating coverage.

### Exemplary Method  
In an exemplary method, a confectionery product is conveyed toward a coating station. A flowable coating material is held in a receptacle and is maintained at a selected temperature and viscosity. The coating material is allowed to flow from the receptacle into a coating void. The confectionery product is positioned adjacent to or partially within the coating void such that only a predetermined portion of the product is exposed to the coating material.  

The coating material contacts the exposed portion and forms a coating layer thereon. The product is then moved away from the coating void while unexposed regions of the product remain substantially uncoated. Excess coating material may drain back into the coating void or into a collection receptacle. The partially coated product is subsequently cooled or otherwise treated to set the coating.

### Advantages  
Embodiments of the invention may provide one or more of the following advantages:

1. Accurate application of coating material to selected product regions.  
2. Reduced coating waste compared with full enrobing followed by removal.  
3. Reduced need for mechanical masking or wiping.  
4. Ability to coat sides, bottoms, edges, ends, or localized regions of confectionery products.  
5. Compatibility with continuous or indexed production lines.  
6. Ability to apply different coating materials from multiple receptacles.  
7. Improved repeatability of coating boundaries and coating thickness.  
8. Simplified cleaning by using removable receptacles and coating void components.  

### Example Claims  

#### Claim 1  
A device for applying a partial coating to a confectionery product, the device comprising:  
a product support configured to support the confectionery product;  
at least one receptacle configured to contain a flowable edible coating material; and  
a coating void fluidly connected to the at least one receptacle and positioned relative to the product support such that, when the confectionery product is supported by the product support, coating material flowing from the at least one receptacle into the coating void contacts only a predetermined portion of the confectionery product to form a partial coating thereon.

#### Claim 2  
The device of claim 1, wherein the coating void is at least partially defined between a forming member of the device and a surface of the confectionery product.

#### Claim 3  
The device of claim 1, wherein the at least one receptacle is arranged above the coating void such that the coating material flows into the coating void by gravity.

#### Claim 4  
The device of claim 1, further comprising a pump, valve, metering device, or dosing element configured to control flow of the coating material from the at least one receptacle to the coating void.

#### Claim 5  
The device of claim 1, wherein the coating void comprises a channel, recess, cavity, gap, trough, or chamber shaped to define a boundary of the partial coating.

#### Claim 6  
The device of claim 1, wherein at least one dimension of the coating void is adjustable to vary a thickness, height, width, or area of the partial coating.

#### Claim 7  
The device of claim 1, further comprising an overflow or return passage configured to remove excess coating material from the coating void.

#### Claim 8  
The device of claim 1, wherein the product support comprises a conveyor, carrier, pocket, tray, gripper, or mold plate configured to move the confectionery product relative to the coating void.

#### Claim 9  
The device of claim 1, wherein a plurality of receptacles is provided, each receptacle being configured to supply a respective coating material to the coating void or to a respective coating void.

#### Claim 10  
The device of claim 1, wherein the coating material comprises chocolate, compound coating, icing, glaze, caramel, fat-based coating, sugar-based coating, yogurt coating, or a combination thereof.

#### Claim 11  
A method for applying a partial coating to a confectionery product, the method comprising:  
positioning the confectionery product relative to a coating void;  
supplying a flowable edible coating material from at least one receptacle into the coating void;  
contacting only a predetermined portion of the confectionery product with the coating material in the coating void; and  
separating the confectionery product from the coating void such that the predetermined portion carries a partial coating and another portion of the confectionery product remains substantially uncoated.

#### Claim 12  
The method of claim 11, wherein supplying the coating material comprises allowing the coating material to flow from the at least one receptacle into the coating void by gravity.

#### Claim 13  
The method of claim 11, wherein the confectionery product is conveyed continuously past the coating void.

#### Claim 14  
The method of claim 11, wherein the confectionery product is indexed into a coating position adjacent to the coating void and subsequently indexed away from the coating void.

#### Claim 15  
The method of claim 11, further comprising controlling a level of coating material in the coating void using an overflow, weir, sensor, valve, or pump.

#### Claim 16  
The method of claim 11, further comprising adjusting a dimension of the coating void to alter the partial coating.

#### Claim 17  
The method of claim 11, further comprising collecting excess coating material from the coating void and returning the excess coating material to the at least one receptacle.

#### Claim 18  
The method of claim 11, further comprising cooling, drying, crystallizing, or setting the partial coating after the confectionery product is separated from the coating void.

### Industrial Applicability  
The invention is applicable to the manufacture of confectionery products requiring controlled localized coating, including chocolate bars, filled bars, cereal bars, biscuits, wafers, pralines, candy pieces, snack products, frozen confectionery articles, and decorative confectionery products. The device and method may be integrated into continuous production lines or used as a standalone coating station.
